summary: Describes how a pseudowire can carry PPP or HDLC units over an MPLS network without terminating the PPP/HDLC protocol. Service providers can offer emulated HDLC or PPP link services over existing MPLS networks. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of building a separate old-style line, the provider packs its traffic inside a modern network, as if the old line were still there.

questions: how does ppp over mpls work
what is the pseudowire control word
subtitle: Carrying PPP and HDLC links across an MPLS network as pseudowires, without ending the link protocol.

tldr.problem: Service providers want to offer emulated HDLC or PPP link services over their existing MPLS networks without terminating the PPP or HDLC protocol.
tldr.mechanism: A pseudowire carries each PPP/HDLC packet inside MPLS, behind a pseudowire label and an optional four-byte control word. HDLC drops flags and the FCS, and PPP also drops the HDLC framing.
tldr.outcome: The service is not a perfect emulation of a real PPP or HDLC link, and some PPP options such as FCS alternatives, ACFC and ACCM do not work if negotiated.

sections.title: Pseudowires for PPP and HDLC
sections.content:
A pseudowire (PW) carries PPP or HDLC Protocol Data Units over an MPLS network without terminating the PPP/HDLC protocol. The RFC assumes the PW has already been set up, either by manual configuration or by a signaling protocol such as the one in RFC 4447.

The model comes from RFC 3985. A customer edge (CE) device connects over an attachment circuit to a provider edge (PE) router. PE1 encapsulates the packet, the network transports it, and PE2 decapsulates it and sends it out on its attachment circuit. Quality of service issues are not discussed in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Two offices think they are joined by a private cable. In truth, the provider tucks their messages into its own network and takes them out at the far end.

sections.title: What the Service Does and Does Not Emulate
sections.content:
The RFC says this service is not intended to emulate traditional PPP or HDLC service perfectly. Notable differences: packet ordering can be preserved only with the OPTIONAL sequence field, a Frame Relay port mode or HDLC PW does not process Frame Relay status messages or alarms, and HDLC flags are processed locally in the PE connected to the attachment circuit.

Because HDLC mode passes packets in a largely transparent way, any protocol with HDLC-like framing can use it, including PPP, Frame Relay and X.25. Exceptions are cases that need direct access to the flags, the FCS or bit/byte unstuffing.

For PPP, media-specific framing is not carried, so three options do not work if the peers negotiate them: FCS alternatives, Address-and-Control-Field-Compression (ACFC) and Asynchronous-Control-Character-Map (ACCM). PW MTU negotiation is also not affected by the PPP MRU, so a PDU longer than the PW allows is discarded by the ingress router.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a good copy of the old line, not a perfect one. A few fancy tricks the old line allowed will not work through the copy.

sections.title: Encapsulation and the Control Word
sections.content:
The packet is built from a PSN transport header, a pseudowire header (with MPLS, this is the label at the bottom of the label stack), a control word and the PPP/HDLC payload.

The 32-bit control word is based on RFC 4385. It starts with four zero bits, then four flag bits that MUST be 0 on send and ignored on receipt, then 2 bits defined in RFC 4623, a 6-bit length and a 16-bit sequence number. If the packet length (payload plus control word) is under 64 bytes, the length field MUST hold it, so the egress PE can strip padding; otherwise it MUST be zero. Sequence number 0 means unsequenced, and processing the field is OPTIONAL.

The control word is optional, since early implementations had none, but new implementations MUST be able to send and receive packets without it. The egress PE MUST know whether the ingress PE will send one, by configuration or signaling. One reason to use it is ECMP: a PPP protocol number starting with 0x4 or 0x6 could be mistaken for an IPv4 or IPv6 packet and sent down a different path.
sections.plainLanguage: The control word is a small sticker on the front of each parcel. It can say how long the parcel really is and what number it is in the sequence, so nothing gets muddled.

sections.title: HDLC, Frame Relay Port and PPP Modes
sections.content:
HDLC mode carries the whole HDLC PDU, including the address and control fields but excluding flags and the FCS, and bit/byte stuffing is undone. It uses PW type 0x0006. Frame Relay port mode is optional and uses the same encapsulation but PW type 0x000F; all Frame Relay virtual circuits on a port map to one PW, so the PE never sees them individually.

PPP mode uses PW type 0x0007 and carries the PPP PDU in full, including the protocol field, but without HDLC address and control fields or FCS. PPP negotiation status is transparent to the PW and MUST NOT be sent to the remote PE.

In every mode, when the PE sees an attachment circuit status change, such as a link failure or an administrative disable, it MUST send the matching PW status notification. A frame that exceeds the interface MTU MUST be dropped, and PPP devices SHOULD NOT negotiate MRUs larger than the AC MTU.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of parcel: plain old-line frames, bundled Frame Relay lines, and PPP. Each gets its own type number so the far end knows how to unpack it.

sections.title: The MPLS Label and MTU
sections.content:
A 32-bit label stack entry is prepended to the encapsulation and acts as the bottom label, called the PW label. The ingress LSR MUST set its S bit to 1. If quality of service information is carried, it SHOULD be placed in the EXP field of the PW label, and any labels higher in the stack MUST carry the same value.

The network MUST be configured with an MTU large enough for the largest encapsulated packet, which with MPLS is likely 12 or more bytes more than the largest packet. Fragmentation as in RFC 4623 MAY be used; without it, an encapsulated PDU that is too big for the tunnel MUST be dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: The label is the address on the parcel that tells the network which pseudo-cable it belongs to. The network also has to allow parcels a bit bigger than the original message, to fit the labels.

sections.title: Congestion and Security
sections.content:
PPP/HDLC PWs carry an unspecified kind of service, so they cannot behave in a TCP-friendly manner. In the presence of services that reduce their rate, they would take more than a fair share and SHOULD be halted. Whenever possible they should run over traffic-engineered PSNs, and PEs SHOULD monitor for congestion; on significant congestion the PW SHOULD be administratively disabled.

The RFC says the PW type is subject to the general security considerations of RFC 3985 and RFC 4447. It specifies only encapsulations, so the security issues of the protocols carrying the packets are not affected. It has no new IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The pseudo-cable does not slow down when the road is jammed, so it has to be switched off if the network gets too crowded.
